newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe tries to halt party revolt.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe tries to halt party revolt.

text.p: Former prime minister and Gaullist party chief Alain Juppe, under fire after a crushing left-wing victory in France's parliamentary election, said on Tuesday his party would elect a new leader in September.
But Juppe's proposal failed to end calls for his ouster in his Rally for the Republic (RPR) party after Sunday's rout.
"My only concern is the unity of the Gaullist movement," Juppe told a hastily-convened "news conference" at which journalists were told no questions would be allowed.
The gathering was called after more than a dozen senior Gaullists, including former Interior Minister Charles Pasqua, demanded that Juppe be dumped and replaced by his arch-rival Philippe Seguin.

Juppe did not spell out if he would be a candidate to keep the party leadership, but he made clear he had no intention of yielding to growing calls from backers of Seguin, a left-wing Gaullist, for his immediate resignation.
Pasqua said later that Juppe's proposal was "unacceptable". And 26 RPR deputies close to Seguin blasted Juppe's solution.
"Faced with the situation created by the legislative election, The RPR party must renew itself. In this context, calling a congress in September does not respond to the failure of June 1," they said.
Juppe aides admitted the calling of a party congress in September, instead of next year as scheduled, was an exercise in damage control aimed at allowing the situation to cool down.

Juppe said he was appointing former interior minister Jean-Louis Debre, widely respected within the RPR party, as interim secretary-general pending the September congress. He replaces Jean-Francois Mancel who resigned on Monday.
Debre is son of the late prime minister Michel Debre, a historical Gaullist figure who was General Charles de Gaulle's first premier after he returned to power in 1958.

Juppe faced calls for his ouster after the ruling centre-right was crushed by a Socialist-led left-wing coalition, leaving Gaullist President Jacques Chirac a lame duck after disastrously gambling that voters would re-elect the right.
Seguin was quoted on Monday by L'Est Republicain, the main newspaper serving his east France power base, as forecasting blood on the walls in the fight for control of the party.
The daily said Seguin had spoken of a "knife fight to the finish" to wrestle the leadership from Juppe.
Juppe also said the forthcoming congress would "decide on the necessary opening to create a great political force committed to supporting the action of President Jacques Chirac".
This appeared to be the latest in a long series of attempts to create an umbrella body for conservative parties. Past moves to create such a grouping collapsed under rival personal ambitions.

Among leaders of the anti-Juppe movement was Pierre Mazeaud, chairman of the outgoing National Assembly's legal committee, who said: "Philippe Seguin is the only person who can restore the lost confidence of our members, our voters and France."

Chirac has not taken sides publicly but political sources said he was likely to resist Seguin's efforts to take over. Seguin is known to harbour resentement against Chirac for choosing Juppe instead of him as prime minister in 1995.

The burly former National Assembly speaker could well try to use the party machinery to set himself up as a rival or successor to Chirac at the next presidential election in 2002. Chirac is widely assumed to want to stay for a second term.
The jockeying for power in the RPR was mirrored in the upper ranks of the centre-right Union for French Democracy (UDF), the RPR's partner in the former ruling coalition.

UDF leader Francois Leotard said he would stand down as head of the small Rebublican party this month. He said he hoped ex-finance minister Alain Madelin would take over the party, which he has threatened to split. Leotard would stay head of the UDF.

Outgoing Education Minister Francois Bayrou was said keen to establish a separate centrist group in the new parliament, where his Democratic Force party is now bigger than the Republican Party, the UDF's overall head.
But it was later announced Bayrou had agreed to head the UDF parliamentary group, indicating the loose-knit coalition had backed away from a break-up.
